primitives.name: Deep learning theory is organized by three pillars, approximation, optimization, and statistical learning, matching the three error terms of the total error
assumptions: A trained model error can be decomposed into approximation, optimization, and generalization components
The three parts can be analyzed with separate mathematical machinery
primitives.breakdown_regime: The decomposition is an organizing device, not a bound by itself: the terms interact in practice (the optimizer sees only the empirical risk, and the hypothesis class is chosen before data arrives), so pillar-wise optima need not compose into a global optimum.

layer2.mapping: The engine keeps an explicit error budget with three accounts for every learned component: representation error (can the class express the target), search error (did fitting find it), and estimation error (does sample performance transfer). No component is promoted on the strength of one account while another account is unmeasured, because the book's whole structure says total error is the sum of the three.
layer2.telemetry: Per-component ablation and audit reports that attribute held-out error to capacity, optimization, or sample size

primitives.verbatim_quote: The material is structured around the three main pillars of deep learning theory: Approximation theory, Optimization theory, and Statistical Learning theory. This structure, which corresponds to the three error terms typically occuring in the theoretical analysis of deep learning models

primitives.name: Training is empirical risk minimization: average the loss over the sample and minimize it over the network class

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\hat{R}_S: empirical risk of the network on sample S (loss units)

assumptions: Sample S of input-output pairs is given
A loss function L measuring dissimilarity is fixed
The network output depends differentiably on the parameters when gradient methods are used
primitives.breakdown_regime: The empirical risk measures fit at the training points only. Driving it to zero says nothing by itself about unseen inputs, which is the interpolation trap the book formalizes in Chapters 9 and 14.

layer2.mapping: Every fitted engine component is an empirical risk minimizer over a historical sample with an explicit loss. The engine records the sample, the loss, and the achieved empirical risk for each fit, so any later claim about a component can be traced to the exact minimization that produced it, and the gap to population risk is booked separately under the risk decomposition primitive.
layer2.telemetry: Training samples, loss definitions, and achieved empirical risk values per fitted component

primitives.verbatim_quote: A standard way of achieving (1.2.2) is by minimizing the so-called empirical risk of Φ with respect to the sample S

primitives.name: A deep network is a composition of affine maps and componentwise activations, hence a parameterized function class whose parameters are the affine entries

symbol_and_unit_ledger.T_j: affine map of layer j, T_j(x) = W_j x + b_j

assumptions: Layers are feedforward: neurons in layer l+1 read only layer l
The same activation is applied componentwise within a layer
Parameters are exactly the weights and biases of the affine maps
primitives.breakdown_regime: The formalism covers feedforward architectures; recurrence, attention with data-dependent weights, and weight sharing need the extensions of Chapter 17, and the realization map it induces is nonlinear in the parameters even though each layer is affine in its input.

layer2.mapping: The engine's reasoning stack has the same shape: layers of evidence transforms composed in sequence, with the parameter vector being the full set of transform coefficients. Treating the stack as one parameterized class, rather than as unrelated heuristics, is what makes capacity, training, and generalization analysis applicable to the whole stack at once.
layer2.telemetry: The engine's layer graph, its coefficient inventory, and intermediate activations on logged cases

primitives.verbatim_quote: Similar to a single neuron, (deep) neural networks can be viewed as a parameterized function class, with the parameters being the entries of the matrices and vectors determining the affine transformations

primitives.name: ReLU has derivative zero or one, which limits vanishing gradients, but a neuron whose preactivation stays negative is dead: constant output and zero gradient, untrainable by gradient methods
assumptions: ReLU activation
Gradient-based training
The dead case arises when a bias makes the unit output zero for all inputs, as in the book's example with negative bias
primitives.breakdown_regime: ReLU is not differentiable at zero, is unbounded above, and passes negative evidence by deleting it entirely; a dead unit is a stationary point, so gradient training cannot revive it from that configuration.

layer2.mapping: Any gated unit in the engine can die the same way: if a situation gate's threshold regime makes its output constant across all observed cases, its gradient signal is zero and downstream fitting treats it as absent. The engine therefore monitors per-gate activation rates and flags a silent gate as a failed sensor to be repaired, never as evidence that the gated factor does not matter.
layer2.telemetry: Per-gate activation frequency, output variance, and gradient magnitude across logged cases

primitives.verbatim_quote: Since its derivative is always zero or one, it does not suffer from the vanishing gradient problem to the same extent as the sigmoid function. However, ReLU can suffer from the so-called dead neurons problem.

primitives.name: Shallow networks are universal approximators of continuous functions if and only if the activation is not a polynomial (Theorem 3.9)
assumptions: Activation in the class M of Definition 3.1 (measurable, not a.e. polynomial in the book's setup)
Arbitrary width is allowed
Approximation is uniform on compact sets for continuous targets
primitives.breakdown_regime: The theorem is qualitative: it gives no rate, no width bound, and no way to find the weights. The book itself warns that such existence results leave the practically relevant questions open, which is why the later chapters replace it with rates.

layer2.mapping: Representation possibility is not the engine's binding constraint: a wide enough shallow readout can approximate any continuous evidence-to-projection map. Design effort therefore goes to approximation rates, sample sizes, and trainability, and a failed fit is never excused by claiming the class could not express the target without a rate argument attached.
layer2.telemetry: Width versus held-out approximation error curves for engine readout classes

primitives.verbatim_quote: Then Nd1 (σ; 1) is a universal approximator of C 0 (Rd ) if and only if σ is not a polynomial.

primitives.name: Kolmogorov superposition: every continuous multivariate function is a sum of 2d+1 compositions of univariate functions, a fixed depth-2, width O(d^2) representation (Theorem 3.21)
primitives.page: Ch. 3, Sec. 3.2, Theorem 3.21 and discussion, text lines ~1716-1900

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\varphi_{i,j}: univariate inner functions, independent of f

assumptions: Target continuous on a compact cube
Inner functions can be chosen independently of the target
Exact representation, not approximation
primitives.breakdown_regime: The inner and outer univariate functions can be extremely rough and hard to approximate themselves, and the companion superexpressive activation result (Proposition 3.20) encodes all rational polynomials into one activation. The book concludes these results have highly limited practical relevance; they are possibility results, not constructions.

layer2.mapping: The theorem licenses the engine's additive factor architecture in principle: a multivariate projection can be decomposed into per-factor univariate response curves combined by an outer sum. The engine uses the decomposition as a structural prior for interpretability, while heeding the book's warning that the univariate pieces may be rough, so their fitted smoothness is measured rather than assumed.
layer2.telemetry: Fitted univariate factor curves and their measured roughness (variation, Lipschitz estimates)

primitives.verbatim_quote: Kolmogorov's superposition theorem is intriguing as it shows that approximating d-dimensional functions can be reduced to the (generally much simpler) one-dimensional case through compositions.

primitives.name: N-term B-spline superposition approximates C^k functions at rate C N^{-k/d}: accuracy epsilon needs order epsilon^{-d/k} parameters, exponential in dimension (Theorem 4.3, Remark 4.4)
primitives.page: Ch. 4, Sec. 4.1, Theorem 4.3 and Remark 4.4, text lines ~1996-2010

symbol_and_unit_ledger.B_i: multivariate cardinal B-splines of order n from Definition 4.1
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c_i: superposition coefficients, bounded by C times the sup norm of f

assumptions: Target in C^k([0,1]^d) with 0 < k at most n, the spline order
Coefficients uniformly bounded as stated
Uniform (sup norm) error on the unit cube
primitives.breakdown_regime: The rate is the curse of dimensionality in concrete form: for fixed smoothness the parameter cost of accuracy grows exponentially in d, and the bound is an upper bound whose constant depends on the C^k norm of the target.

layer2.mapping: Smooth response surfaces in the engine are priced by this rate: a claimed fit quality for a k-smooth surface over d inputs implies a basis budget of order epsilon^{-d/k}. The engine refuses to certify a smooth high-dimensional fit whose term count cannot support its claimed accuracy, and reports the implied budget next to the fit.
layer2.telemetry: Basis term counts, fitted smoothness order, and sup-norm residuals of engine response surfaces

primitives.verbatim_quote: The number of parameters N determines the approximation accuracy N −k/d . This implies that achieving accuracy ε > 0 requires O(ε−d/k ) parameters (according to this upper bound), which grows exponentially in d.

primitives.name: Networks with higher-order sigmoidal activations match the spline rate C N^{-k/d} with size at most C N and depth logarithmic in d and k (Theorem 4.9)
primitives.page: Ch. 4, Sec. 4.2, Theorem 4.9 and discussion, text lines ~2226-2260

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi_N: neural network with sigmoidal activation of order q

assumptions: Sigmoidal activation of order q at least 2
Target in C^k with 0 < k at most n and n at least 2
Depth is the ceiling of log base 2 of d plus the ceiling of log base q of (k-1)
primitives.breakdown_regime: Parity with splines means networks inherit the spline rate including its curse of dimensionality; nothing here beats N^{-k/d}, and the construction uses higher-order sigmoidals rather than the ReLU used in practice.

layer2.mapping: The engine loses nothing by using learned readouts instead of hand-built spline tables for smooth response surfaces: same rate, comparable parameter count, and depth that grows only logarithmically in smoothness. Readout choice is therefore made on auditability and data fit, not on approximation power.
layer2.telemetry: Parameter counts and sup residuals of spline-table versus network readouts on the same surfaces

primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 4.9 shows that neural networks with higher-order sigmoidal functions can approximate smooth functions with the same accuracy as spline approximations while having a comparable number of parameters.

primitives.name: Every continuous piecewise linear function with n affine pieces is exactly a ReLU network, of size, width order d n 2^n and depth order n (Theorem 5.7)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi_f: ReLU network realizing the cpwl function f exactly
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of affine pieces of f (count)

assumptions: Target continuous and piecewise linear with n affine pieces
Domain convex
Exact realization, no approximation error
primitives.breakdown_regime: The generic construction is exponential in the number of pieces, so exact conversion of a hand-built piecewise linear rule can be far larger than the rule itself; structured cases (triangulations, Theorem 5.14) do better, but arbitrary cpwl surfaces do not.

layer2.mapping: Hand-built piecewise linear scoring surfaces and learned ReLU components live in one hypothesis space: each can be audited against the other exactly. The engine keeps both forms for important surfaces, converts when an audit needs it, and budgets the conversion cost, which can be exponential in piece count, before promising an exact translation.
layer2.telemetry: Piece counts and converted sizes of the engine's piecewise linear surfaces

primitives.verbatim_quote: Then, there exists a ReLU neural network Φf such that Φf (x) = f (x) for all x ∈ Ω and size(Φf ) = O(dn2n ), width(Φf ) = O(dn2n ), depth(Φf ) = O(n).

primitives.name: Every cpwl function on a convex domain has a max-min representation: a maximum over minima of its affine pieces (Proposition 5.8, eq. 5.2.1)
primitives.page: Ch. 5, Sec. 5.2, Proposition 5.8, eq. (5.2.1), text line ~2658

symbol_and_unit_ledger.g_i: the n affine pieces of f
symbol_and_unit_ledger.s_j: index subsets of the affine pieces

assumptions: Target cpwl with n affine pieces as in Definition 5.5
Domain convex
primitives.breakdown_regime: The representation is exact but not unique and not necessarily small; the number of max terms can grow combinatorially, and minima of affine functions are concave, so the form exposes structure without making optimization convex.

layer2.mapping: Max-min form is the engine's interpretable normal form for scenario logic: the outer maximum selects the governing scenario and the inner minimum is the binding constraint inside it. Any piecewise linear engine surface can be rewritten this way so a human can read which scenario and which constraint produced a given output.
layer2.telemetry: Scenario counts and binding-constraint identities logged per engine output

primitives.verbatim_quote: Then there exists m ∈ N and sets sj ⊆ {1, . . . , n} for j ∈ {1, . . . , m}, such that f (x) = max min(gi (x)) for all x ∈ Ω.

primitives.name: A cpwl network of depth L has at most (p times width)^L pieces: width grows pieces polynomially, depth exponentially (Theorem 6.3); matching lower bounds force error at least C (2 width)^{-2L} (Theorem 6.4)
primitives.page: Ch. 6, Sec. 6.1, Theorems 6.3 and 6.4, text lines ~3560-3620

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p: number of pieces of the activation function (2 for ReLU)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Pieces(\\Phi): number of affine regions of the realized function (count)

assumptions: Activation continuous piecewise linear with p pieces
Univariate input and output for the stated form
Upper bound is worst case over parameters
primitives.breakdown_regime: The bound counts what an architecture could realize, not what trained parameters do realize; Chapter 6.3 shows typical random networks sit far below it, so the bound must not be quoted as realized capacity.

layer2.mapping: Depth is the engine's regime-multiplication dial: when a reasoning surface needs many distinct linear regimes, adding depth multiplies regime capacity while adding width only adds to it polynomially. Capacity plans for engine surfaces are therefore written in terms of depth first, with width sized to the per-regime complexity.
layer2.telemetry: Architecture depth and width of engine surfaces, with realized region counts measured on sampled inputs

primitives.verbatim_quote: While increasing the width can polynomially increase the number of pieces, increasing the depth can result in exponential increase. This is a first indication of the prowess of depth of neural networks.

primitives.name: Randomly initialized deep networks have far fewer pieces than the maximum: along a segment the expected piece count grows essentially linearly in depth times total neurons, not exponentially (Theorem 6.9, Remark 6.10)
primitives.page: Ch. 6, Sec. 6.3, Theorem 6.9 and Remark 6.10, text lines ~3850-4030
assumptions: Random biases and weights with the maximal internal derivative bounded as in Definition 6.8
Expectation over the random initialization
Pieces counted along a unit line segment through the domain
primitives.breakdown_regime: The result is about initialization, not trained networks, and it needs the internal derivative control that standard initialization schemes are designed to provide; adversarially chosen weights can still approach the exponential bound.

layer2.mapping: Capacity claims in the engine are calibrated to measured, realized complexity rather than architecture maxima. A deep component is not credited with exponential expressivity by default; its realized region count is measured at initialization and after fitting, and only the measured number enters capacity arguments.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical linear-region counts along sampled segments, at initialization and after fitting

primitives.verbatim_quote: This shows that in expectation, the number of pieces is linear in the number of layers, as opposed to the exponential upper bound of Theorem 6.3.

primitives.name: Depth approximates the square function exponentially fast: the sawtooth construction s_n has depth n, width 3, size at most 7n, and sup error at most 2^{-2n-1} (Lemma 7.2)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.s_n: piecewise linear interpolant of x^2 at 2^n breakpoints, realized as a ReLU network
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: number of sawtooth compositions, equal to depth (count)

assumptions: Domain [0,1]
ReLU activation
s_n is the linear interpolant of the square at dyadic breakpoints
primitives.breakdown_regime: The construction is specific to the square on [0,1] and its iterates; it is the engine inside the multiplication and polynomial results, not a general approximation scheme by itself, and shallow networks provably cannot match it (Theorem 6.4).

layer2.mapping: Quadratic interaction terms in the engine are implemented with small deep units rather than wide shallow ones, because this lemma prices a quadratic at single-digit size per binary digit of accuracy. When an engine component needs a product-like nonlinearity, depth is spent here first.
layer2.telemetry: Approximation error of engine quadratic units versus their depth

primitives.verbatim_quote: In conclusion, we have shown that sn : [0, 1] → [0, 1] approximates the square function uniformly on [0, 1] with exponentially decreasing error in the neural network size.

primitives.name: Multiplication of two numbers is approximable to accuracy epsilon by a ReLU network of size and depth order 1 + |log epsilon|, via the polarization identity and the square construction (Lemma 7.3)
primitives.page: Ch. 7, Sec. 7.2, Lemma 7.3, eq. (7.2.1), text lines ~4223-4260

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi^\\times_\\varepsilon: ReLU network approximating the product with sup error at most epsilon

assumptions: Inputs in [-1, 1]
Polarization identity reduces product to squares
The approximant is exactly zero when either factor is zero
primitives.breakdown_regime: Cost grows logarithmically in accuracy but the construction is for scalar products on a bounded range; unbounded ranges need rescaling, and n-fold products (Proposition 7.4) pay a binary-tree overhead per additional factor.

layer2.mapping: Multiplicative interactions between evidence factors are cheap in the engine and are never linearized away for cost reasons: a product of two bounded factors costs size logarithmic in the accuracy target. Wherever the reasoning says two effects multiply, the implementation multiplies, with the accuracy budget stated.
layer2.telemetry: Product-unit sizes and sup errors for engine interaction terms

primitives.verbatim_quote: We start with the multiplication of two numbers, in which case neural networks of logarithmic size in the desired accuracy are sufficient, [332, Proposition 3].

primitives.name: Analytic non-linear functions are approximable by deep ReLU networks at an exponential rate: size at most N and depth order sqrt(N) give sup error at most C exp(-beta sqrt(N)) (Proposition 7.6)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi_N: deep ReLU network with size at most N and depth at most C sqrt(N)

assumptions: Target analytic on [-1, 1] and not linear
Univariate case as stated
Constants depend on the target's Taylor coefficients
primitives.breakdown_regime: Analyticity is a strong assumption: merely smooth or piecewise smooth targets fall back to the polynomial rates of Theorem 7.11, and the constants degrade as the analyticity radius shrinks toward the interval.

layer2.mapping: Very smooth, physics-like response components in the engine are expected to fit nearly exactly at modest size. When such a component fits poorly, this result redirects suspicion from capacity to the data or the smoothness premise itself, and the audit asks which of those failed before any size is added.
layer2.telemetry: Fit residuals of smooth engine subcomponents as a function of allocated size

primitives.verbatim_quote: Let f : [−1, 1] → R be analytic but not linear. Then there exist constants C, β > 0 such that for every N ∈ N, there exists a ReLU neural network ΦN such that

primitives.name: Depth separation: for analytic non-linear targets, deep networks reach error epsilon exponentially fast in size while every depth-at-most-L network has error at least C^{-1} size^{-2L} (Corollary 7.8)
primitives.page: Ch. 7, Sec. 7.3, Corollary 7.8, eqs. (7.3.2) and (7.3.3), text lines ~4495-4515

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi_{\\mathrm{shallow}}: any ReLU network of depth at most L
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C: constant depending on the analytic target f

assumptions: Target analytic and non-linear on [-1, 1]
Lower bound holds for every shallow network, uniformly
Upper bound is Proposition 7.6
primitives.breakdown_regime: The separation is proven for specific target classes; it does not say depth helps for every function, and for fixed small L the shallow lower bound still decays polynomially, so shallow models are inefficient here rather than useless.

layer2.mapping: Persistent underfitting by a shallow engine head on a structured target is treated as architecture evidence, not signal absence: this corollary is the standing justification for answering a shallow failure with depth before concluding the underlying pattern is not there.
layer2.telemetry: Shallow versus deep parameter counts at equal held-out error for engine heads

primitives.verbatim_quote: The proposition shows that the approximation of certain (highly relevant) functions requires significantly more parameters when using shallow instead of deep architectures. Such statements are known as depth separation results.

primitives.name: Deep ReLU networks approximate C^{k,s} functions at rate C N^{-(k+s)/d} with size order N log N and depth order log N, by partition of unity, local Taylor polynomials, and approximate multiplication (Theorem 7.11)
primitives.page: Ch. 7, Sec. 7.4, Theorem 7.11, eq. (7.4.3), text line ~4628

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C^{k,s}: Hölder space of functions with k derivatives and s-Hölder highest derivative
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi_N: ReLU network of size order N log N and depth order log N
symbol_and_unit_ledger.(k+s)/d: rate exponent: total smoothness over dimension

assumptions: Target in C^{k,s} on the unit cube
Construction: uniform mesh, partition of unity, local Taylor polynomials, approximate multiplication by Lemma 7.3
The earlier cpwl route (Theorem 5.23) gives the Hölder case with bounded depth
primitives.breakdown_regime: Up to logarithmic factors the rate equals the spline rate, so depth does not beat the curse for generic smooth classes; it only matches the optimal rate with a more flexible class, and the constant depends on d, k, s and the target norm.

layer2.mapping: This construction is the engine's local-expert pattern made precise: partition the state space into cells, fit a simple local model in each cell, blend with a partition of unity, and multiply factors approximately. The theorem prices the pattern: total error scales as N^{-(k+s)/d}, so cell count and local smoothness jointly determine what accuracy a local-expert design can claim.
layer2.telemetry: Cell counts, per-cell local fit errors, and blend weights in engine local-expert components

primitives.verbatim_quote: The idea of the proof is to use the so-called "partition of unity method": First we will construct a partition of unity (φν )ν , such that for an appropriately chosen M ∈ N each φν has support on a O(1/M ) neighborhood of a point η ∈ Ω.

primitives.name: Curse of dimensionality as a lower bound: the continuous nonlinear N-width of the C^k unit ball is at least C_k N^{-k/d}, so any network with continuous weight selection needs N at least (C_k/epsilon)^d parameters for accuracy epsilon (Theorem 8.4, Corollary 8.6)
primitives.page: Ch. 8, Sec. 8.1.2, Theorem 8.4, Corollary 8.6, eq. (8.1.5), text lines ~5080-5140

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\gamma_{k,d,N}: continuous nonlinear N-width of the C^k unit ball, eq. (8.1.4)

assumptions: Weight selection map W from targets to parameters is continuous
Worst case over the whole C^k unit ball
Holds for every architecture, activation, and sparsity pattern
primitives.breakdown_regime: Continuity of the weight selection is essential: with discontinuous selection, space-filling pathologies (and the superexpressive activation of Chapter 3) make the width zero. The bound is a worst-case statement about a whole smoothness ball, not about any one structured target.

layer2.mapping: This is the engine's impossibility filter: any claim of dimension-free accuracy on an unstructured smooth class is rejected on sight, and the claimant must name the structural assumption (compositionality, manifold support, Barron-type spectrum) that exempts the target from the lower bound. No structural assumption, no exemption.
layer2.telemetry: Accuracy claims logged with their parameter counts, dimensions, and named structural assumptions

primitives.verbatim_quote: The statement shows again a curse of dimensionality: for any continuous weight selection process, and any neural network architecture of size at most N ∈ N, the best achievable uniform approximation is lower bounded by Ck N −k/d .

primitives.name: Barron class: functions with bounded first Fourier moment are approximable by one-hidden-layer networks with mean-square error at most c/N on the unit ball, with no dimension factor in the rate (Theorem 8.12)
primitives.page: Ch. 8, Sec. 8.2, Theorem 8.12, eq. (8.2.1), text lines ~5335-5480

symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Gamma_C: Barron class: functions whose representing density g satisfies the integral of |xi| |g(xi)| at most C

assumptions: Target in the Barron class Gamma_C for some finite C
Sigmoidal activation
Error measured in mean square over the unit ball, not uniformly
primitives.breakdown_regime: The constant C can itself grow with dimension (the book's Exercise 8.21 gives a Gaussian in Gamma of order sqrt(d)), the guarantee is mean-square rather than uniform, and membership in the class is a real restriction that many targets fail.

layer2.mapping: The engine screens candidate target surfaces for Barron-type spectral decay before choosing a head: where the first Fourier moment is finite and moderate, a shallow wide head is statistically cheap even in high dimension; where the moment is huge or infinite, the curse pricing of the spline and width results applies instead.
layer2.telemetry: Spectral moment estimates of target surfaces and the head architectures chosen for them

primitives.verbatim_quote: Importantly, the dimension d does not enter on the right-hand side of (8.2.1), in particular the convergence rate is not directly affected by the dimension, which is in stark contrast to the results of the previous chapters.

primitives.name: Compositional functions on a directed acyclic graph whose nodes consume at most m inputs are approximable at rate N^{-(k+s)/m}: the maximal node arity, not the ambient dimension, sets the rate (Sec. 8.3)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.F_M: compositional target built on a DAG with M vertices
symbol_and_unit_ledger.m: maximal number of ingoing edges per vertex (count)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi_{F_M}: ReLU network of size order N log N

assumptions: Each node function fj has C^{k,s} norm at most 1
Graph is acyclic with one output vertex
Node functions depend on at most m variables each
primitives.breakdown_regime: The constant depends on the graph size M and on m, k, s; if some node consumes many inputs the rate degrades toward the ambient curse, and the result presumes the compositional structure is real, not imposed on a target that lacks it.

layer2.mapping: This is the design law for the engine's reasoning graph: keep every node's input arity small. A pipeline of narrow compositions inherits the rate of its widest node, so the engine audits the graph by maximal arity and refactors any node that silently accumulates inputs, because that node alone sets the price of the whole graph.
layer2.telemetry: Reasoning graph arity distribution and per-node approximation errors

primitives.verbatim_quote: As a next instance of types of functions for which the curse of dimensionality can be overcome, we study functions with compositional structure. In words, this means that we study high-dimensional functions that are constructed by composing many low-dimensional functions.

primitives.name: Functions on a smooth compact m-dimensional manifold in R^d are approximable at rate C N^{-(k+s)/m}: the intrinsic dimension m, not the ambient d, sets the rate (Proposition 8.18)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.M: smooth compact m-dimensional manifold in R^d
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi_f^N: ReLU network of size order N log N and depth order log N

assumptions: Manifold smooth and compact, covered by finitely many tangent projection charts
Target C^{k,s} on the manifold, measured chartwise
Error measured only on the manifold
primitives.breakdown_regime: Constants depend on the manifold's geometry (chart count, curvature scale delta), and the rate says nothing off the manifold: inputs that leave the data manifold are outside the guarantee entirely.

layer2.mapping: The engine budgets parameters against the intrinsic dimension of its state representation, not the raw feature count. State embeddings are therefore built and audited for low intrinsic dimension, and any input that falls off the training manifold is flagged as out-of-guarantee rather than extrapolated silently.
layer2.telemetry: Intrinsic dimension estimates of state representations and off-manifold distance flags for live inputs

primitives.verbatim_quote: Another instance in which the curse of dimension can be mitigated, is if the input to the network belongs to Rd , but stems from an m-dimensional manifold M ⊆ Rd . If we only measure the approximation error on M, then we can again show that it is m rather than d that determines the rate of convergence.

primitives.name: Optimal reconstruction under a Lipschitz bound: the average of the upper and lower cone envelopes through the data is a worst-case optimal, interpolating reconstruction (Theorem 9.4)
primitives.page: Ch. 9, Sec. 9.2, Theorem 9.4, eq. (9.2.6), text lines ~6350-6450
primitives.latex: \Phi(x) := \frac{1}{2} \left( f^{\mathrm{upper}}(x) + f^{\mathrm{lower}}(x) \right), \quad f^{\mathrm{upper}}(x) := \min_{k} \left( y_k + M \|x - x_k\| \right), \quad f^{\mathrm{lower}}(x) := \max_{k} \left( y_k - M \|x - x_k\| \right)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.M: assumed Lipschitz constant bound, at least the data-implied minimum of eq. (9.2.3)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.\\Phi: optimal reconstruction, itself M-Lipschitz and interpolating

assumptions: Target is M-Lipschitz with M at least the slope implied by the data pairs
Reconstruction quality judged by worst-case sup error over all such targets
Data values are exact

reasoning_traces.think:
This book is a mathematical theory of deep learning, and its first move is organizational: everything a trained network does wrong is charged to one of three accounts, approximation, optimization, or statistical estimation, and the seventeen chapters are those three accounts audited in order. That framing matters because it forbids a common confusion. A model that fails might lack the capacity to express the target, might own the capacity but never find the right parameters, or might fit the available sample perfectly while saying nothing about unseen cases. The book insists these are different failures with different mathematics, and it proves theorems about each under assumptions stated sharply enough to be checked.
The approximation part begins with possibility and immediately replaces it with price. Universal approximation (Theorem 3.9) says a shallow network with a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function, and the book treats this as the start of the subject rather than its triumph, because it carries no rate. Rates arrive through splines: N spline terms buy error N^{-k/d} for a C^k target, and the exponent already contains the curse of dimensionality, since accuracy epsilon costs on the order of epsilon^{-d/k} parameters. Networks with higher-order sigmoidal activations match the spline rate exactly (Theorem 4.9), so the first honest statement of the theory is that the flexible class inherits the classical price. Exactness results sharpen the picture of what ReLU networks are: they are precisely the continuous piecewise linear functions (Theorem 5.7), every such function has a max-min normal form (Proposition 5.8), and the number of linear pieces is the currency in which expressivity is counted. Depth multiplies that currency exponentially while width only adds polynomially (Theorem 6.3), yet typical random networks realize only a piece count linear in depth and size (Theorem 6.9), an early warning that worst-case capacity and realized capacity are different quantities.
The engine room of the positive results is Chapter 7. A width-3, depth-n sawtooth network approximates the square function with error 2^{-2n-1} (Lemma 7.2); the polarization identity turns squares into products at logarithmic cost (Lemma 7.3); products build polynomials; polynomials plus a partition of unity build the optimal smooth rate N^{-(k+s)/d} with only logarithmic depth (Theorem 7.11). Along the way sit the results that justify depth as more than a heuristic: analytic targets are approximable at the exponential rate exp(-beta sqrt(N)) (Proposition 7.6), while every shallow network pays a polynomial lower bound on the same targets (Corollary 7.8), a clean depth separation. Then Chapter 8 turns the theory around and proves what cannot be done. For any continuous way of assigning parameters to targets, the worst-case error over a smoothness ball is at least C_k N^{-k/d} (Theorem 8.4, via Borsuk-Ulam), so the curse is not an artifact of a bad construction but a property of continuous parameterization itself. The escapes from the curse are therefore the most valuable statements in the book, and each one names a structure: a bounded first Fourier moment (Barron class, rate c/N free of dimension in the rate), compositional structure with small node arity (rate governed by m, not d), or data supported on a low-dimensional manifold (rate governed by intrinsic dimension). Kolmogorov superposition and the superexpressive activation serve as controlled warnings in the other direction: representation theorems whose inner functions are arbitrarily rough, or whose parameters cannot be found by any stable procedure, are mathematically true and practically empty, and the book says so in plain words.
The optimization part starts from the convex ideal, where gradient descent converges linearly at a rate set by the condition number (Theorem 10.7) and stochastic gradient descent reaches order 1/k error only when update variance is driven down (Theorem 10.10). Real network losses are not convex, so the book studies the landscape directly. A shallow network with at least as many hidden units as samples has no spurious valleys (Proposition 12.4); the set of functions a fixed architecture realizes is the image of parameter space under a locally Lipschitz map whose constant degrades exponentially with depth (Proposition 13.1); and that function set is typically non-convex with arbitrarily large holes (Theorem 13.9), which is why best approximations can fail to exist and weights can grow without bound during training. The bridge back to tractability is width. The empirical tangent kernel concentrates on a deterministic limit (Theorem 11.20), and for sufficiently wide networks gradient descent provably tracks the training of the linearized model and reaches global minima of the square loss (Theorems 11.13 and 11.28). In that regime the trained network is, up to a vanishing gap, a kernel machine, which explains both its trainability and its limits: feature learning is precisely what the linearization leaves out.
The statistical part closes the loop. Empirical risk minimization splits excess risk into twice a generalization term plus an approximation term (equation 14.2.2), and the generalization term is controlled by covering numbers, which for sparse bounded networks scale with the active parameter count times depth (Theorems 14.15 and 14.16), or by VC dimension, of order n_A L log n_A for ReLU classes (Theorem 14.28). Those classical bounds then meet their own boundary: networks can interpolate arbitrary labels (Chapter 9), the optimal use of data under a mere Lipschitz assumption is an explicit max-min envelope (Theorem 9.4), and past the interpolation threshold the risk can descend a second time (Chapter 15), so interpolation is not by itself a verdict. Finally the book prices fragility: an adversarial perturbation is an explicit gradient step whose size is the margin divided by the gradient norm (Theorem 16.8), tying robustness to the same Lipschitz quantities that governed stability in Chapter 13.
For a reasoning engine the transfer is direct. Budget error in three accounts and never let one account's success hide another's debt. Keep every node's input arity small, because arity, not ambient dimension, sets the achievable rate for compositional structure. Measure realized complexity rather than quoting architecture maxima. Treat depth as the multiplier of representational regimes and width as the additive term. Score every decision boundary by margin over gradient norm before trusting its label. Combine models at the prediction level, never by averaging weights into a hole in function space. And refuse, on the authority of the width lower bound, any accuracy claim that does not name the structure exempting it from the curse of dimensionality.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage is explicit in the book's own bibliography discussions. Universal approximation descends from Cybenko, Hornik, and Funahashi in the late 1980s to the Leshno, Lin, Pinkus and Schocken characterization the book proves as Theorem 3.9. Kolmogorov's superposition theorem dates to 1957 and its practical relevance has been debated ever since. The spline rate machinery comes from classical approximation theory, the sawtooth and multiplication constructions from Yarotsky's 2017 work, and depth separation from Telgarsky. The nonlinear width lower bounds follow DeVore and collaborators, with Borsuk-Ulam as the topological engine. Barron's class is from 1993, the neural tangent kernel from Jacot, Gabriel and Hongler in 2018, residual networks from He and collaborators in 2015, double descent from Belkin and collaborators, and adversarial examples from Szegedy and collaborators. The book's contribution is consolidation: one notation, one set of definitions, and the classical and modern results made to confront each other.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors write as mathematicians who believe that deep learning practice has outrun its justification, and that the remedy is not skepticism but sharper statements. Their philosophy, stated in the outline section, is to prioritize provable statements presented with simplicity and clarity over generality, illustrating ideas in special cases under strong assumptions when that is what honesty requires. Their model of the reader is someone who will check the proofs and who distrusts an existence claim that arrives without a rate, a constant, or a procedure for finding the weights. They consistently treat the assumptions of a theorem as part of the theorem: continuity of the weight selection map, boundedness of the weights, finiteness of a Fourier moment. Where the field tells itself comforting stories, about capacity, about interpolation, about robustness, their instinct is to ask what the words mean precisely, and then let the resulting statement be a theorem or a counterexample, whichever it turns out to be.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The book's layers veto each other in ways an engine designer must respect. The nonlinear width lower bound vetoes any approximation claim that cannot name a structural escape, no matter how good the construction looks. The covering number and VC results veto trust in a fitted component whose active complexity dwarfs its sample, however low its training error sits. The interpolation results veto the inference from training fit to generalization, and the typical-pieces theorem vetoes capacity arguments built from worst-case region counts. In the other direction, the no-spurious-valleys and linearization results veto blaming local minima for failures of overparameterized or wide components, redirecting the audit to data and loss design. The adversarial margin formula vetoes confidence in any boundary whose gradient norm is large relative to its margin. Each veto is a case of one part of the theory constraining what another part is permitted to assert.

universal_lens: Strip the domain away and the book is a general audit template for any parameterized prediction system. Ask three questions in order. What can the class express, and what does accuracy cost in the complexity budget, given the dimension of the input and the smoothness or structure of the target. Can the parameters actually be reached by the search procedure in use, and what does the geometry of the parameter-to-function map do to stability along the way. Does success on the observed sample certify anything off the sample, and at what sample size relative to the class's complexity. Then apply the book's standing warning: possibility is cheap, and any claim that escapes a lower bound must name the structural assumption that exempts it. A discipline that cannot separate its approximation, optimization, and estimation accounts does not yet know why its systems work.
gsi_mapping: The institute takes this book as its audit standard and its taxonomy for learning methods. Every method admitted to the institute corpus is filed by pillar, approximation, optimization, or statistics, with its structural assumption named in plain language, its convergence or approximation rate stated in the budget it consumes, and its breakdown regime recorded beside the claim rather than in a footnote. The three proven escapes from the curse of dimensionality, Barron-type spectral decay, compositional structure with small node arity, and low intrinsic dimension of the data support, become the institute's classification of when high-dimensional learning is legitimate at all. The lower bounds, nonlinear widths, VC dimension, and the adversarial margin formula, become rejection criteria: a result that cannot say which side of them it lives on is not yet a result the institute will teach.
gse_mapping: The engine takes operational rules, each traceable to a theorem. Error is budgeted in three accounts per component, so a failure is charged to capacity, search, or sample before it is charged to the model. The reasoning graph keeps node arity small, because maximal arity sets the approximation rate for everything downstream. Parameter budgets are set against measured intrinsic dimension rather than raw feature count. Multiplicative interactions are implemented as products, since depth makes them logarithmically cheap, and local structure is handled by partition-of-unity experts whose cell counts are priced by the smooth rate theorem. Decision boundaries carry a fragility score, margin over gradient norm. Ensembles combine predictions, never weights. And no component is promoted on training fit alone, because interpolation and generalization are separate facts in this theory.
